title: Exposure: title and occasion
short: Based on the winter of 1916-17 on the Somme, when Owen's platoon lay out in the snow; the poem was begun in December 1917 and revised in 1918.
body: In January 1917 Owen's battalion held front-line positions near Beaumont Hamel and Serre on the Somme in one of the coldest winters on record. On 4 February he wrote to his mother that his platoon had no dug-outs and had to lie in the snow 'under the deadly wind', and that one man froze to death. The Oxford archive says the poem was begun at Scarborough in December 1917, revised there in early 1918 and completed in France in September 1918; one draft page carries a puzzling date ('Feb. 1916'), which may be a slip for 1917 or 1918. 'Exposure' means both lying unprotected in the open and dying of cold. The enemy in the poem is the weather, not the Germans.

anchor: iced east winds that knife us
title: merciless iced east winds that knife us
short: The east wind attacks like a bayonet: nature takes the place of the enemy soldier.
body: The verb 'knife' turns the wind into an assailant with a blade, and 'merciless' gives it a will. Throughout the poem the weather behaves like an army (dawn 'attacks', the air is 'deadly'), while actual combat is distant ('some other war'). The long, heavy lines, with their slow stresses and trailing ellipses, enact the exhausted waiting of the sentries. Owen also uses the first person plural throughout, so the experience is collective.

sources.cite: Wilfred Owen, The Complete Poems and Fragments, ed. Jon Stallworthy (Chatto & Windus / Hogarth Press / Oxford UP, 1983)

title: Pararhyme
short: Owen rhymes on consonants with changed vowels (silent/salient, wire/war, snow/renew): an unresolved, disquieting music.
body: Owen's innovation is pararhyme (also called consonantal or half rhyme): words whose consonants match but whose stressed vowels differ, as in silent/salient, wire/war, brambles/rumbles, grow/gray, faces/fusses, burn/born, us/ice. Each five-line stanza rhymes ABBA on these partial chimes, followed by a short refrain line. The ear expects a full rhyme and gets a dissonance, and the effect suits a poem of frustration and unresolved suspense. Edmund Blunden's memoir in his 1931 edition of the poems drew early attention to these assonances, and Owen is now regarded as the technique's chief pioneer in English.

title: the salient
short: A salient is a section of front line that juts out into enemy territory, exposed on three sides.
body: In military usage a salient is a bulge in the front line projecting toward the enemy, and therefore vulnerable to fire from several sides; the Ypres Salient was the most notorious of the war. 'Low drooping flares' are star-shells fired to light up no man's land; as they fall they distort the familiar shapes, so the sentries' 'memory of the salient' is confused. The word pararhymes with 'silent' in the previous line.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'salient, n.'

title: But nothing happens
short: The short refrain closes four of the eight stanzas: the futile waiting of trench warfare, which kills without battle.
body: Each stanza ends with a short, indented line. 'But nothing happens' recurs four times (stanzas 1, 3, 4 and 8), and the other refrains vary it with questions and statements ('What are we doing here?', 'Is it that we are dying?', 'We turn back to our dying.', 'For love of God seems dying.'). The refrain makes boredom and futility the poem's subject. In military terms the night is uneventful, yet men are dying of cold. The last 'But nothing happens' is the bitterest: by then the burial party is at work.

title: twitching agonies of men among its brambles
short: The wind-tugged barbed wire recalls the death throes of men caught and killed on the wire.
body: The 'wire' is the barbed-wire entanglement in front of the trench, and its 'brambles' are the coils of barbed wire, a grim pastoral metaphor. The gusts tugging at it make it twitch like the bodies of men dying on it, a sight familiar from failed attacks. The simile introduces dying men into a stanza where, officially, nothing happens. The full stop after 'wire' (where a comma might be expected) is in the text here.

sources.cite: Wilfred Owen, The Complete Poems and Fragments, ed. Jon Stallworthy (Chatto & Windus / Hogarth Press / Oxford UP, 1983)

title: What are we doing here?
short: The refrain becomes a question about the purpose of the war itself, answered only later and ambiguously.
body: Hearing the guns rumble 'northward' like 'a dull rumour of some other war' (the distant fighting elsewhere on the front), the soldiers question their own presence. The colloquial phrasing is a soldier's grumble and also a profound question about the war's meaning. Stanza 7 offers a strained, ambiguous answer: they lie out here because otherwise the fires of home could not burn.

title: Dawn ... her melancholy army
short: Dawn, traditionally the hour of attack, is an army of grey clouds; the real assault comes from the weather.
body: Dawn was the usual hour for attacks ('stand-to' at first light). Here Dawn herself is the attacker, massing grey clouds in ranks as an enemy masses troops. The personification inverts the classical rosy-fingered Dawn of Homer into a 'melancholy army'. Again nothing happens in human terms. The line also echoes the opening's 'east winds': the east was where the German lines lay.

sources.cite: Wilfred Owen, The Complete Poems and Fragments, ed. Jon Stallworthy (Chatto & Windus / Hogarth Press / Oxford UP, 1983)
Homer, Odyssey 2.1 and passim ('rosy-fingered Dawn')

title: Less deadly than the air
short: The bullets are less deadly than the cold: the poem's central claim, taken from Owen's own experience.
body: The bullets streaking the silence are real danger, yet the air 'that shudders black with snow' is deadlier. Owen's letter of 4 February 1917 used the same adjective for the 'deadly wind' under which his platoon lay. The snowflakes are rendered with soft sibilants and liquids (sidelong, flowing, flakes, flock), and their lazy beauty is set against their lethal effect. 'Nonchalance' gives the wind an indifference that matches the God of the later stanzas.

title: Pale flakes with lingering stealth (textual)
short: Sassoon's 1920 text reads 'lingering'; most modern texts (following the manuscripts) read 'fingering stealth'.
body: This archive follows the first edition, edited by Siegfried Sassoon (1920), which prints 'lingering stealth'. Later editions read 'fingering stealth', which fits the touch of 'come feeling for our faces': the snowflakes are like fingers groping in the dark, uncanny and stealthy. The text here is therefore mixed: in stanza 7 it prints 'Nor ever suns', the corrected reading of later editions, where Sassoon's 1920 text has 'Now ever suns'. Owen's manuscripts survive in several drafts, and Stallworthy's edition records their readings.

sources.cite: Poems by Wilfred Owen, ed. Siegfried Sassoon (Chatto & Windus, 1920; reprinted 1921)

title: snow-dazed ... sun-dozed
short: A pararhyme pivots from the snow-dazed present to a sun-drowsy dream of spring ditches, blossoms and blackbirds.
body: The compound pair snow-dazed / sun-dozed is itself a pararhyme and a hinge. The freezing men, crouching in their holes, drift ('drowse') into memory or hallucination of English spring: grassy ditches, blossom, a blackbird fussing. The dream is gentle and pastoral, and its drowsiness is also the drowsiness of hypothermia, which is why the refrain asks 'Is it that we are dying?'

title: Slowly our ghosts drag home
short: In a vision the soldiers' ghosts return home but find the doors shut; they are already strangers to it.
body: The dying men's spirits 'drag' home, an exhausted verb. They see the fire, crickets and mice, a cosy domestic interior in which the house now belongs to the mice: the household has gone on without them. The shutters and doors are closed, and the repeated 'closed' turns literal into figurative: home is shut against those who have been sent away to die. The refrain 'We turn back to our dying' accepts the exclusion.

sources.cite: Wilfred Owen, The Complete Poems and Fragments, ed. Jon Stallworthy (Chatto & Windus / Hogarth Press / Oxford UP, 1983)

title: glozed
short: A rare word: probably 'glazed', 'glossed' and 'glowing' at once, describing embers with a crust of dark-red jewels.
body: 'Gloze' in standard English means to gloss, explain away or flatter, and it is related to 'gloss'. Owen seems to use it for the sheen of the sunken fire: embers that glow under a glaze of ash, 'crusted dark-red jewels'. Editors note that it is a rare, possibly coined usage. The sound also prepares the pararhyme with 'closed' at the end of the stanza.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'gloze, v.'

title: Since we believe not otherwise can kind fires burn
short: The hardest stanza: the soldiers lie out here because they believe their sacrifice keeps home and God's spring alive.
body: The syntax is compressed. The men believe that only through their sacrifice can the 'kind fires' of home burn, and suns shine on child, field and fruit. So they lie out 'not loath' (not unwilling), as if born for it. 'For God's invincible spring our love is made afraid' is the crux. It may mean that the men's love fears for the renewal of the world in spring that they are defending, or that they fear spring itself, which will come whether they live or not. The refrain 'For love of God seems dying' can mean that God's love for them, or their love of God, is failing. Critics differ on whether the stanza expresses genuine conviction or bitter irony at patriotic religion.

sources.cite: Wilfred Owen, The Complete Poems and Fragments, ed. Jon Stallworthy (Chatto & Windus / Hogarth Press / Oxford UP, 1983)

title: His frost
short: The frost is God's: the capital 'His' makes the deity responsible for the cold that kills.
body: With 'His frost', the God of 'God's invincible spring' becomes the agent of death. The frost will 'fasten' on mud and men alike, shrivelling hands and puckering foreheads. Owen had once been a lay assistant to an evangelical vicar, at Dunsden (1911-13), and lost much of his faith there. The poem's theology is one of indifference or hostility, echoing the 'nonchalance' of the wind.

sources.cite: Dominic Hibberd, Wilfred Owen: A New Biography (Weidenfeld & Nicolson, 2002)

title: The burying-party ... half-known faces
short: Soldiers detailed to bury the frozen dead hesitate over faces they half recognise; their own eyes are ice.
body: A burying-party was a work detail assigned to collect and bury the dead. The cold makes them shake, and they 'pause over half-known faces', the faces of comrades half recognisable, or distorted by frost. 'All their eyes are ice' refers ambiguously to the dead (frozen eyes) or to the burial party (numbed beyond feeling), and the pararhyme us/ice closes the poem in the sound. Then the refrain returns, 'But nothing happens', at its most ironic: men are dead and the official record notes no action.
